statements.eye-as-a-single-thin-lens: The cornea and lens of the eye can be treated as a single thin converging lens a fixed distance from the retina, on which it forms a real, inverted image. The thin lens equations then describe the eye, and every defect and correction becomes a question about that one lens.
statements.cornea-supplies-most-of-the-power: The largest change in refractive index, and so the greatest bending of light, is where light passes from air into the cornea, so the cornea supplies about two-thirds of the power of the eye and the lens the rest. This is why reshaping the cornea corrects vision.
statements.accommodation: Accommodation is the ability of the eye to adjust its focal length. Because the lens-to-retina distance is fixed, the eye focuses on objects at different distances by changing the power of its lens.
statements.thin-lens-equations-for-the-eye: Written in terms of power, the thin lens equation for the eye is $P = 1/d_{\text{o}} + 1/d_{\text{i}}$, with the image distance fixed at the lens-to-retina distance, and the magnification is $h_{\text{i}}/h_{\text{o}} = -d_{\text{i}}/d_{\text{o}}$.
statements.solve-for-an-image-on-the-retina: To find the power the eye needs or the size of an image on the retina, set the image distance to the lens-to-retina distance, put every distance in meters, and apply the thin lens equations for the eye.
statements.presbyopia: Presbyopia is a condition in which the lens of the eye becomes progressively unable to focus on objects close to the viewer, as the ability to accommodate shrinks with age. It is a loss of added power for close vision, and a converging lens supplies the missing power.
statements.myopia-and-hyperopia: Nearsightedness, or myopia, is a visual defect in which distant objects appear blurred because their images are focused in front of the retina; the eye has too much power. Farsightedness, or hyperopia, is the condition in which incoming rays reach the retina before they converge into a focused image; the eye has too little power for close objects.
statements.near-point-and-far-point: The far point is the object point imaged on the retina by an unaccommodated eye, normally at infinity. The near point is the point nearest the eye at which an object is accurately focused on the retina at full accommodation, normally 25 cm away.
statements.correct-nearsightedness: A diverging lens corrects nearsightedness by making an image of a distant object at the person's far point. Its power follows from the thin lens equation, with the image distance negative and measured from the spectacle.
statements.correct-farsightedness: A converging lens corrects farsightedness by making an image of a close object at the person's near point, farther away than the object itself. Measure both distances from the spectacle and give the image distance its negative sign.
statements.astigmatism: Astigmatism is the result of an inability of the cornea to focus an image properly onto the retina, a difference in the power of the eye along different axes. It is corrected with a cylindrical lens rather than a spherical one.
statements.powers-of-close-lenses-add: The power of thin lenses placed close together is approximately the sum of their powers. This lets a contact lens, a tear layer or a reshaped cornea be treated as an addition to the power of the eye.
statements.laser-vision-correction: Laser vision correction is a medical procedure that corrects myopia, hyperopia and astigmatism by reshaping the cornea, which supplies most of the power of the eye. The laser uses ultraviolet light, which the cornea absorbs strongly.
statements.rods-and-cones: Rods and cones are the two types of photoreceptors in the human retina. Rods are sensitive and colorless and serve vision at low light levels; cones are active at higher light levels, give color and fine detail, and crowd the fovea.
statements.simplified-theory-of-color-vision: The simplified theory of color vision states that there are three primary colors, which correspond to the three types of cones, each sensitive to a different range of wavelengths. It explains how three colors of light can produce thousands of hues, though some evidence shows that it is incomplete.
statements.true-color-of-an-object: The true color of an object is set by the wavelengths it absorbs and reflects, a property of the object rather than of the light falling on it. From it we can predict how a colored object appears under light that is not white.
statements.color-of-a-light-source: The color of a light source is set by the spectrum of wavelengths it emits, from the sharp line of a laser to the broad spectrum of the Sun.
statements.color-constancy: Color constancy is the part of the visual perception system that lets people perceive color consistently in a variety of conditions, so that a white tablecloth looks white under sunlight and under candlelight. The eye and brain achieve it by comparing an object with its surroundings.
statements.compound-microscope: A compound microscope is constructed from two convex lenses, the objective and the eyepiece. The objective forms a large real image, and that image is the object for the eyepiece, which magnifies it further as a magnifier does.
statements.overall-magnification: The overall magnification of a system of thin lenses and mirrors is the product of the magnifications of its elements, $m = m_{\text{o}}m_{\text{e}}$, since each element multiplies the height of the image it is given.
statements.solve-a-multiple-element-system: To find the image and magnification of a system of two or more lenses, locate the image formed by the first lens, use its distance from the second lens as that lens's object distance, and so find the final image and the overall magnification.
statements.numerical-aperture: The numerical aperture of a lens, $\text{NA} = n \sin\alpha$, expresses its ability to gather light and to resolve fine detail, where $n$ is the index of refraction of the medium between the lens and the specimen and $\alpha$ is half the angle of acceptance.
statements.f-number: The $f$-number of a camera lens is its focal length divided by the diameter of its aperture, $f/\# = f/D \approx 1/(2\,\text{NA})$. A smaller $f$-number means a wider aperture and more light.
statements.immersion-objectives: Filling the gap between the specimen and the objective with oil or water lets rays that would have been refracted away enter the lens, which makes the numerical aperture larger than one.
statements.microscopes-beyond-visible-light: A specimen must be illuminated by transmission, scattering or reflection, and microscopes that use x rays or electrons in place of light resolve far finer detail with the same focusing physics.
statements.distant-image-at-the-focal-length: For an object at a very great distance, the thin lens equation puts the image one focal length behind the objective, which fixes where the eyepiece of a telescope goes.
statements.angular-magnification-of-a-telescope: The angular magnification of a telescope with two convex lenses is $M = \theta'/\theta = -f_{\text{o}}/f_{\text{e}}$, so a large magnification needs an objective of long focal length and an eyepiece of short focal length.
statements.upright-and-inverted-telescopes: A telescope of two convex lenses forms an inverted image. Galileo's concave eyepiece, or a third convex lens that inverts the image again, gives an upright one.
statements.reflecting-telescopes: A concave mirror can serve as the objective of a telescope. Mirrors can be made far larger than lenses, gather more light, reach long focal lengths and do not suffer from chromatic aberration.
statements.telescopes-across-the-spectrum: Telescopes are not limited to visible light: radio dishes and grazing-incidence x-ray mirrors extend them across the electromagnetic spectrum.
statements.chromatic-aberration: Chromatic aberration is the dependence of the focal length of a lens on the color of the light. Because the index of refraction depends on wavelength, a single lens brings violet light to a focus closer than red. Mirrors are free of it, and a doublet of two glasses partly corrects it.
statements.coma-and-spherical-aberration: Coma is the failure of rays from an off-axis object to meet at one point. Spherical aberration is the focusing of rays through the edge of a lens closer than rays near its axis. Both occur even in light of one color.
statements.correcting-aberrations: Aberrations are reduced by stopping down the aperture, by shaped surfaces, by systems of several elements, by graded index lenses and by correcting the image with a computer, at a cost in brightness or complexity.

new.name: Hue
new.statement: The hue of a color is its identity as it relates specifically to the spectrum, such as red, orange or blue.

new.name: The retinex theory of color vision
new.statement: The retinex theory explains color and brightness perception and their constancies as the work of both the retina and the cortex, whose names combine in its own. It accounts for the ability to perceive color in an ambient-colored environment.

new.name: Objective lens
new.statement: The objective lens of an optical instrument is the lens nearest to the object being examined.

new.name: Eyepiece
new.statement: The eyepiece of an optical instrument is the lens or combination of lenses nearest to the eye of the observer.

new.name: Angular magnification, $M = \theta'/\theta$
new.statement: The angular magnification of an instrument is the ratio of the angle the image subtends at the eye to the angle the object subtends when viewed by the unaided eye.

new.name: Adaptive optics
new.statement: Adaptive optics is an optical technology in which computers adjust the lenses and mirrors of a device to correct rapidly changing distortions of the image, such as those the atmosphere causes in a telescope.

new.name: Aberration
new.statement: An aberration is a failure of rays to converge at one focus because of limitations or defects in a lens or mirror.

new.name: Myopia, or nearsightedness
new.statement: Myopia, or nearsightedness, is a visual defect in which distant objects appear blurred because their images are focused in front of the retina rather than on it.

new.name: Hyperopia, or farsightedness
new.statement: Hyperopia, or farsightedness, is the condition of an eye in which incoming rays of light reach the retina before they converge into a focused image, so that close objects appear blurred.

new.name: Near point
new.statement: The near point is the point nearest the eye at which an object is accurately focused on the retina at full accommodation, normally 25 cm away.

new.name: Far point
new.statement: The far point is the object point imaged on the retina by an unaccommodated eye, normally at infinity.
